\section[\texorpdfstring{\fa{غمگین} (ghamgin)}{غمگین (ghamgin)}]{\fa{غمگین} (ghamgin) — sad, sorrowful}

\label{lesson:FA-C484-ghamgin}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Persian for to lie, then the Persian for a liar.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \fa{غمگین}}
\textbf{\fa{غمگین}} (\emph{ghamgin}) — \textquotedblleft{}sad, sorrowful\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\fa{او} \fa{بعد} \fa{از} \fa{رفتن} \fa{دوستش} \fa{غمگین} \fa{بود}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{u ba'd az raftan-e dustash ghamgin bud.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
She was sad after her friend left.
\end{quote}

\emph{gham} 'sorrow' + the adjective ending \emph{-gin}. More literary than \emph{nârâhat}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{ghamgin} is built in Persian on \emph{gham}, 'sorrow', which was borrowed from Arabic \emph{ġamm} (EtymDB), with the native adjective ending \emph{-gin}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ghamgin}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{ghamgin}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Persian for to lie, then the Persian for a liar, then say \emph{ghamgin} again

\section[\texorpdfstring{\fa{غم} (gham)}{غم (gham)}]{\fa{غم} (gham) — sorrow, grief}

\label{lesson:FA-C484-gham}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Persian for a liar, then the Persian for sad.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \fa{غم}}
\textbf{\fa{غم}} (\emph{gham}) — \textquotedblleft{}sorrow, grief\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\fa{او} \fa{غم} \fa{بزرگی} \fa{در} \fa{دل} \fa{دارد}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{u gham-e bozorgi dar del dârad.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
She carries a great sorrow in her heart.
\end{quote}

Short and often poetic. \emph{gham khordan} — to grieve.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{gham} was borrowed from Arabic \emph{ġamm}, 'grief, distress' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{gham}, once more

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Persian for a liar, then the Persian for sad, then say \emph{gham} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\fa{غصه} \fa{خوردن} (ghosse khordan)}{غصه خوردن (ghosse khordan)}]{\fa{غصه} \fa{خوردن} (ghosse khordan) — to fret; to grieve}

\label{lesson:FA-C484-ghosse-khordan}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Persian for sad, then the Persian for sorrow.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \fa{غصه} \fa{خوردن}}
\textbf{\fa{غصه} \fa{خوردن}} (\emph{ghosse khordan}) — \textquotedblleft{}to fret; to grieve\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\fa{مادربزرگ} \fa{برای} \fa{همه} \fa{غصه} \fa{میخورد}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{mâdarbozorg barâ-ye hame ghosse mikhorad.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Grandmother frets about everyone.
\end{quote}

\emph{ghosse} 'grief' + \emph{khordan} 'to eat': 'to eat grief'. Present stem \emph{khor-}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{ghosse} was borrowed from Arabic \emph{ġuṣṣa}, 'distress, pang' (EtymDB); Hindi \emph{gussa} 'anger' is usually traced to the same word. \emph{khordan}, 'to eat', is inherited Persian.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Persian for sad, then the Persian for sorrow, then say \emph{ghosse khordan} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\fa{افسرده} (afsorde)}{افسرده (afsorde)}]{\fa{افسرده} (afsorde) — depressed, low}

\label{lesson:FA-C484-afsorde}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Persian for sorrow, then the Persian for to fret.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \fa{افسرده}}
\textbf{\fa{افسرده}} (\emph{afsorde}) — \textquotedblleft{}depressed, low\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\fa{او} \fa{در} \fa{زمستان} \fa{کمی} \fa{افسرده} \fa{میشود}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{u dar zemestân kami afsorde mishavad.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
He gets a little low in winter.
\end{quote}

The past participle of \emph{afsordan} 'to wither, to freeze'. The noun is \emph{afsordegi} 'depression'.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{afsorde} is built on the native Persian verb \emph{afsordan}, 'to wither, to freeze': a withered mood. EtymDB has no entry for it, and its older form is not settled.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\fa{پشیمان} (pashimân)}{پشیمان (pashimân)}]{\fa{پشیمان} (pashimân) — sorry, regretful}

\label{lesson:FA-C484-pashiman}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Persian for to fret, then the Persian for depressed.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \fa{پشیمان}}
\textbf{\fa{پشیمان}} (\emph{pashimân}) — \textquotedblleft{}sorry, regretful\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\fa{او} \fa{از} \fa{حرفش} \fa{پشیمان} \fa{شد}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{u az harfash pashimân shod.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
He regretted what he had said.
\end{quote}

\emph{az chizi pashimân shodan} — to come to regret something. The noun is \emph{pashimâni}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{pashimân} is a native Persian word, usually traced to Middle Persian \emph{pašēmān}. EtymDB has no entry for it, so the link is hedged.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
